profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Raleigh) is located at 5150 McCrimmon Parkway #423, Morrisville, NC 27560. The operator publishes a footprint of 99976 square feet and 4.31 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, HITRUST, ISO 27001, SSAE 18. North Carolina's data center demand has grown sharply: Duke Energy's projected additional capacity need rose from about 3.9 gigawatts in early 2024 to nearly 6 gigawatts by May 2025, roughly equivalent to four nuclear plants, according to Canary Media's reporting. Major projects driving that growth include Amazon Web Services' $10 billion, 800-acre campus in Richmond County, billed as the largest single capital project in North Carolina history; an Apple site in Catawba County included in the company's broader $500 billion US expansion; four new Microsoft data centers planned near Charlotte; and an expansion of Google's Caldwell County facility. Duke has won regulatory approval for a large new fleet of gas plants despite state decarbonization requirements, prompting a policy debate among clean-energy advocates who favor load flexibility, utility-scale solar and battery storage, virtual power plants, and clean-transition tariffs as alternatives; a North Carolina Utilities Commission proceeding was scheduled for October 2025 to examine these competing approaches, with timeline pressure driven partly by neighboring Virginia's data center construction pace of 18 months or less.

Duke Energy has separately sought a 15% North Carolina rate increase over two years, on top of bills that had already risen about 22% since 2020, and data centers, currently less than 1% of peak energy use but projected to eventually account for roughly 80% of future demand growth and about 30% of upcoming development projects statewide, have become central to the resulting rate debate, per reporting citing Environmental Defense Fund policy director Will Scott. Scott has argued new power plants built to serve data centers should be paid for through special fees on those large customers rather than socialized across all ratepayers, while Duke spokesperson Bill Norton has disputed that data centers are driving the increases, attributing them instead to infrastructure maintenance and arguing that industrial growth broadly helps spread fixed costs over a larger customer base.

reading.body:
The Flexential Raleigh facility in Morrisville, North Carolina publishes 4.31 MW of critical load UPS capacity across approximately 100,000 square feet, making it the second-largest facility by power in the state among those with disclosed figures.

At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this capacity would support roughly 100 racks. The published power figure does not specify current occupancy or workload type, so it cannot be confirmed whether this infrastructure is currently serving AI deployments or capable of doing so. The facility holds multiple compliance certifications including PCI DSS, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HITRUST, which qualify it for regulated workloads but do not indicate AI-specific capabilities or constraints.

North Carolina has 19 mapped data center facilities statewide, but only five publish power capacity data. Flexential Raleigh accounts for 8.6 percent of the state's 50.3 MW of disclosed critical IT load. This modest share means the facility alone does not reflect regional grid strain or emerging AI infrastructure density. The overall picture in North Carolina remains incomplete because fourteen facilities do not publish their power figures.
